name: Pennsylvania DMV Permit Test
trademarkNotice: This practice resource is independent and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT). The agency's name is used only to identify the test this material helps you prepare for.

examInfo.format: 18 multiple choice questions on traffic signs, Pennsylvania driving laws, and safe driving practices. PennDOT does not post a time limit for the knowledge test, so this practice mock uses 20 minutes. This practice mock uses 4 answer choices per question.

passCriteria.description: You must answer at least 15 of the 18 questions correctly.

content.eligibility: You can apply for a Pennsylvania learner's permit on or after your 16th birthday. You must pass a vision screening and the knowledge test, and applicants under 18 need a parent or guardian's consent. Check the PennDOT Driver and Vehicle Services website for the current forms, documents, and fees before you go.
content.intro: The Pennsylvania permit test is the knowledge test you take to get a learner's permit. It has 18 multiple choice questions on traffic signs, Pennsylvania driving laws, and safe driving practices, and you pass with at least 15 correct answers. The questions are based on the Pennsylvania Driver's Manual. If you do not pass, you may take the test again on the next business day.
content.trendSummary: The test mixes traffic signs with driving laws. Sign shapes and colors, signals and pavement markings, right of way at intersections, school bus and emergency vehicle rules, speed limits, parking distances, the junior license rules, and Pennsylvania's alcohol limits are the topics new drivers most often need to review. The chapters on this site follow the Driver's Manual but are study groupings, not official test sections.
content.studyTip: Start with signs, signals, and pavement markings, because they are the biggest chapter. Then practice right of way, followed by the chapters full of numbers: speed and parking, the junior license rules, and alcohol limits. Redo every missed question the next day, and before test day take a full 18-question Mock Exam and aim for at least 16 correct.

faqs.question: What score do I need to pass the Pennsylvania permit test?
faqs.answer: You need at least 15 correct answers out of 18. That means you can miss no more than 3 questions.

faqs.question: What happens if I fail the knowledge test?
faqs.answer: PennDOT says you may take the knowledge test again on the next business day. Use the time to review the chapters where you missed questions.

faqs.question: How long must I hold my permit before the road test?
faqs.answer: If you are under 18, you must hold your learner's permit for six months and complete at least 65 hours of supervised driving, including at least 10 hours at night and 5 hours in bad weather. A parent or guardian must certify those hours.

faqs.question: Are these the real Pennsylvania test questions?
faqs.answer: No. Every question here is an original practice question written from the rules in the Pennsylvania Driver's Manual and Pennsylvania law. Use this site to learn the rules and read the official manual as well.

studyTips.studyOrder: Start with Signs, Signals, and Pavement Markings, because it is the biggest chapter and the other chapters build on it. Next study Right of Way and Intersections, then Speed, Passing, and Parking and Safe Driving. Finish with the Learner's Permit and Junior License chapter and Alcohol, Implied Consent, and Points, which are short but full of numbers.
studyTips.hardChapters: Speed, Passing, and Parking has many distances that are easy to mix up, such as 15 feet from a fire hydrant, 20 feet from a crosswalk, and 30 feet from a stop sign, so keep them in one list. The junior license chapter has hours, months, a curfew, and passenger limits that change after six months. Alcohol, Implied Consent, and Points uses blood alcohol limits that differ by age and vehicle type.
studyTips.examDay: You need at least 15 correct answers out of 18, so you can miss no more than 3 questions. Read every answer choice before you pick one, because wrong choices often differ by a single number or word. If a question is hard, think about which choice keeps pedestrians and other drivers safest.
